klo: Recognise systemic conditions that constrain strategic execution and organisational progress.
Distinguish visible performance symptoms from their underlying organisational causes.
Evaluate the interdependent enterprise conditions that contribute to stalled or declining performance.
Determine the organisational response required to restore strategic coherence and performance momentum.

sections.label: Facilitator Guide
sections.sub: Orientation, facilitation questions, tone guidance, and watch points for the full unit.

guidance: ◆ Unit Intent

Unit 9 sits at a pivotal moment in the S2R® climb. By this point, the strategy is clear, performance expectations are set, and commitments have been secured. Now the gears begin grinding. This unit names that friction precisely — and gives the leadership team the engineering vocabulary and diagnostic discipline to address it.

The central reframe is powerful and must land clearly: a clog is a signal. It indicates where the organisation’s current operating system has not yet adapted to the new strategic direction. Leaders who understand this stop asking “Why are we failing?” and start asking “Where is the system not yet designed to carry the strategy?”
The Clog Clinic in Application is the centrepiece — protect the full 45 minutes. It must use real stalled KPIs. The quality of the diagnostic conversation is the measure of this unit.
◆ Key Facilitation Questions
“Think of a strategy that stalled in your organisation. Was the plan wrong — or was something in the system blocking its flow?”
“When you last named a performance gap, did you name the symptom or the root cause? What’s the difference in your context?”
“Which of the seven clogs is most predictable in your organisation given your current strategic direction? What does that tell you about where to look first?”
“If Cultural Resistance is your diagnosis — is that genuinely a culture problem, or is it a Leadership Avoidance problem that has produced cultural symptoms?”
“You’ve selected a lever. What would have to be true for that lever to actually clear the clog?”
◆ Tone & Watch Points

Watch for: the relief response. When leaders first encounter the clog map, they often feel relieved — they recognise their organisations immediately. The facilitation risk is that the conversation stays at the level of recognition and stalls before diagnosis and intervention. Push past identification: “Recognising it is the start. Now name it precisely and select the lever.”

Watch for: Cultural Resistance overuse. It is the most comfortable diagnosis because it externalises the problem. Challenge it every time: “Is this a culture issue, or is it the downstream consequence of Leadership Avoidance?”

Watch for: lever vagueness. “We need to improve communication” is too vague to act on. A lever is a structural adjustment — a redesigned decision right, a reset KPI, a rebuilt process, a named accountability. Push every group until their intervention is concrete enough to own.
Timing: Awareness and Intelligence can move at pace. Extrapolating benefits from brief functional discussion. Reserve the full 45 minutes for the Clog Clinic — it should not be compressed.

sections.label: Section 1 · Awareness — What
sections.sub: Naming the internal blockages that prevent strategic intent from flowing into execution — and introducing the 7-clog diagnostic map aligned to ABCV Directional Integrity.
slo: Recognise the systemic blockages that widen the gap between strategic intent and execution.
Identify the observable symptoms of friction in execution.

guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Awareness

Open with the scenario: strategy is clear, objectives are defined, performance expectations are in motion — and then the gears begin grinding. The three friction signals (Decision Paralysis, Kinetic Misalignment, Output-Outcome Gap) are the entry point. Invite leaders to identify which of the three they are most frequently experiencing.

The key conceptual shift is from “failure of strategy” to “failure of flow.” Clogs are evidence that the system carrying the plan has not yet adapted. This reframe is essential before moving to the 7-clog map.

Work through the clog map deliberately. Do not rush. Each clog has a distinct observable pattern, a distinct ABCV element it distorts, and a distinct strategic consequence. Encourage leaders to identify which clogs are currently present in their organisation before moving to Intelligence.

parts.title: 1.1 — What is a Strategic Clog?
content: At this point, the strategy is clear. Objectives are defined. Performance expectations are in motion. Then the gears begin grinding.

At its simplest, a Strategic Clog is an internal blockage that prevents strategic intent from flowing into real-world execution. It is the widening gap between what we said we would do and what is actually happening. These are fundamental misalignments where the organisation’s current state — its habits, its structures, its very DNA — works actively against its future goals.
Strategy sets the destination. Flow determines whether you have the power to arrive.

To navigate this phase of the execution climb, leadership must evolve. Designing a brilliant strategy is only the start. The role of the leadership team is to become Engineers of Execution Flow — developing the diagnostic eyes to detect clogs early, before they compound into stalled momentum or declining performance.
Every clog interferes with one or more elements of ABCV Directional Integrity:
Arena — clarity of the problem space and customer end-game
Boundaries — structural, operational, and regulatory constraints
Competition — how the organisation defines alternatives and threats
Value Proposition — how the organisation creates distinct value
When execution is clogged, strategy loses directional integrity — gradually and silently.

System Logic: A clog acts like a pressure distortion point in the system. It redirects effort away from intended outcomes, weakens coherence across functions, and creates misinterpretation of strategic intent.

parts.title: 1.2 — Three Observable Friction Signals
guidance: ◆ Facilitator Prompt

Ask the group: “Which of these three signals is most visible in your organisation right now? Raise your hand for the one you recognise most immediately.” Use the show of hands to calibrate which clog category to explore first in the map below.
content: Despite the clarity of the plan, the reality of the work will periodically be characterised by friction. Three patterns signal that a clog is forming.
Decision Paralysis
Choices that should be instinctive begin taking longer than expected, creating a bottleneck at the top. Leaders hesitate where they should act.
Kinetic Misalignment
Teams move with intensity but pull in different directions, cancelling each other’s efforts. Energy is high; progress is not.
Output–Outcome Gap
Tasks are completed and boxes are checked, but the needle on actual strategic goals isn’t moving. Activity is high; advancement is not.

parts.title: 1.3 — The 7-Clog Diagnostic Map
parts.meta: ABCV-aligned · Select each clog to explore
guidance: ◆ Diagnostic Principle
Ask: “Which ABCV element is being distorted — and by which clog?”
If multiple signals point to Boundaries → structural or decision system issue
If multiple signals point to Arena → capability or strategic participation issue
If multiple signals point to Value Proposition → behavioural or measurement misalignment
If multiple signals point to Competition → speed, responsiveness, or system capability gap
content: Each clog category represents a distinct type of system misalignment. Select each to examine the structural reality, observable patterns, early warning signals, and strategic impact.
Clog 01
Structural Misfit
Boundaries
Structural Reality
Organisational design (roles, reporting lines, decision rights, governance layers) is misaligned to the current strategy. Structure reflects legacy priorities.
Observable Patterns
Bottlenecks at functional handoffs; duplication of work; fragmented ownership of outcomes; breakdown between front-office and back-office; conflicting priorities across functions.
Early Warnings: Increasing coordination time; rising dependency on informal workarounds; escalation frequency increases; unclear ownership of outcomes.

Strategic Impact: The organisation operates within the wrong structural logic. Execution becomes disjointed, coordination costs increase, and strategy cannot move coherently across the enterprise system.
Clog 02
Capability Gaps
Arena
Structural Reality
Critical capabilities (skills, systems, tools, capacity, partnerships) required to deliver the strategy are absent, underdeveloped, or unevenly distributed.
Observable Patterns
Projects stall or slow; over-reliance on key individuals; inconsistent delivery quality; repeated outsourcing of core capabilities; inability to scale execution.
Early Warnings: Missed milestones; uneven performance across similar initiatives; burnout of key talent; increasing rework.

Strategic Impact: The organisation cannot fully operate within its chosen strategic space. The defined arena becomes theoretical — execution lacks the capability backbone required to compete and deliver.
Clog 03
Decision Bottlenecks
Boundaries
Structural Reality
Decision rights are unclear, overly centralised, or embedded in outdated hierarchical processes. Authority is not aligned to execution proximity.
Observable Patterns
Slow approvals; repeated escalation loops; “waiting culture”; overloaded senior leadership; avoidance of decision ownership at middle levels.
Early Warnings: Decision cycle times increase; growing backlog of unresolved issues; repeated agenda items in meetings; teams hesitate to act without approval.
Strategic Impact: Decision flow is constrained, weakening execution rhythm. The organisation loses responsiveness and cannot adapt at the speed required by the strategy or environment.
Clog 04
Misaligned Metrics & Incentives
Value Proposition
Structural Reality
KPIs, scorecards, and reward systems reinforce behaviours that conflict with strategic intent. Legacy metrics remain active post-strategy shift.
Observable Patterns
Functional optimisation over enterprise outcomes; gaming of metrics; resistance to collaboration; short-term delivery at the expense of long-term value.
Early Warnings: High KPI achievement with weak strategic progress; conflicting performance narratives across functions; misalignment between reported success and actual outcomes.
Strategic Impact: Effort is redirected toward what is measured, whether or not it creates value. The organisation produces activity and output without differentiated strategic outcomes.
Clog 05
Cultural Resistance
Value Proposition
Structural Reality
Deeply embedded beliefs, norms, and habits contradict the behavioural shifts required by the strategy. Informal culture overrides formal direction.
Observable Patterns
Reversion to legacy behaviours under pressure; passive resistance; low initiative; compliance without commitment; scepticism toward change.
Early Warnings: Low engagement in strategic initiatives; limited experimentation; silence or avoidance in critical conversations; informal narratives contradicting strategy.

Strategic Impact: The organisation cannot consistently deliver its intended value because behaviour does not align with strategic intent. Cultural inertia preserves the past, weakening transformation capability.
Clog 06
Technology / Infrastructure Lag
Competition
Structural Reality
Legacy systems, fragmented platforms, and poorly integrated infrastructure cannot support execution demands. Data architecture is incomplete or delayed.
Observable Patterns
Manual workarounds; spreadsheet dependency; delayed reporting; poor data visibility; system integration failures; limited automation.
Early Warnings: Data inconsistencies; long reporting cycles; operational errors increase at scale; inability to track real-time performance.
Strategic Impact: The organisation loses execution speed and intelligence. It cannot respond, scale, or compete effectively against more technologically enabled alternatives.
Clog 07
Leadership Avoidance
Arena + Boundaries
Structural Reality
Leaders avoid confronting trade-offs, underperformance, structural misalignment, or difficult decisions required for strategy execution.
Observable Patterns
Persistent unresolved issues; repeated discussions without closure; weak accountability; shifting priorities; lack of enforcement of decisions.
Early Warnings: Recurring strategic issues across multiple cycles; low trust in leadership decisions; ambiguity in direction; declining ownership across teams.
Strategic Impact: Strategic clarity erodes as unresolved tensions accumulate. The organisation drifts between priorities, weakening both strategic focus (Arena) and execution discipline (Boundaries).

sections.label: Section 2 · Intelligence — Why
sections.h2: Why Clogs Are Predictable Features of Execution
sections.sub: Understanding why execution friction is the inevitable consequence of system misalignment — and introducing the 7 Strategic Unclogging Levers as the leadership toolkit for restoring execution flow.
slo: Explain why execution friction is a predictable consequence of strategy stretching the operating system.
Recognise the leadership disciplines that detect and resolve friction early.

guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Intelligence

The ignition point of this section is the mindset shift: from “Why is the strategy failing?” to “Where is the system not yet designed to carry the strategy?” This is a fundamentally different diagnostic posture that moves leadership from blame to engineering.

Spend time on the pressure point examples — they make the abstract concrete. A strategy requiring cross-functional coordination will expose structural misfits. A strategy requiring decentralised execution will expose decision bottlenecks. These are predictable, based on the design gap between what the strategy demands and what the system can currently provide.

For the 7 levers: make clear that levers are structural adjustments. Rarely does a single lever clear a clog alone. The diagnostic question is always: which lever combination addresses the root cause?

parts.title: 2.1 — Clogs Are Design Signals
content: When leaders define strategy, they design a future operating direction. When the organisation attempts to execute that strategy, it must do so through today’s operating system — its structure, decision rights, culture, metrics, capabilities, and technology. If any element of this system is misaligned with the new strategic direction, friction will appear. The friction is the natural consequence of system misalignment.

This is why execution breakdowns usually occur because the organisation’s structure, capabilities, behaviours, or systems have not yet adapted to the strategy. The clog is therefore the signal that the system requires adjustment.

Clogs emerge precisely where the strategy stretches the existing system beyond its current design capacity. A strategy requiring rapid cross-functional coordination will expose structural misfits. A strategy dependent on data-driven decisions will reveal capability gaps. A strategy requiring decentralised execution will expose decision bottlenecks. These pressures are predictable.

Experienced leadership teams recognise this. They treat clogs as engineering signals indicating where the organisation must evolve. This transforms the role of the executive team: defining strategic direction and ensuring the organisation’s operating system can carry that direction without excessive friction.

parts.title: 2.2 — Three Disciplines of Execution Engineering
content: Discipline 1
Early Identification
Discipline 2
Accurate Classification
Discipline 3
Targeted Intervention
Detect Signals Before They Compound

Leaders must detect the signals that indicate friction is forming. Bottlenecks, repeated coordination failures, declining execution speed, or growing ambiguity in decision rights are all early indicators that a clog is emerging.

The strategic value of early identification is significant. A clog detected when it is a friction signal requires a targeted structural adjustment. The same clog discovered six months later, after it has compounded into a systemic execution failure, requires a crisis response. The cost — in time, capital, and leadership credibility — is vastly different.
This discipline requires leaders to build signal literacy: the ability to read organisational patterns as early indicators of structural misalignment.
Name the Clog Precisely Before Intervening

Each clog belongs to a specific category of organisational friction. Structural misfit, capability gaps, decision bottlenecks, misaligned incentives, cultural resistance, technological constraints, or leadership avoidance each require fundamentally different forms of intervention.

The most common diagnostic failure is applying the wrong lever to a correctly identified symptom. A leader who observes “slow execution” and responds by adding resources is applying a capability lever to what may be a decision bottleneck. The additional resources do not accelerate execution because the constraint is approval latency.
Accurate classification requires resisting the impulse to solve before diagnosing. The first question is “What type of friction is this, and what does it tell us about the system?”
Pull the Right Lever with Precision

Once the clog is identified and classified, it must be addressed through the appropriate strategic lever. Clogs rarely clear themselves through trying harder or working more hours. They require a deliberate adjustment to the organisation’s structural, behavioural, and operational settings.

Targeted intervention means matching the lever to the root cause. It also means accepting that rarely does a single clog require just one fix. A Capability Gap may require both Upgrade (systems) and Reinforce (skills). A Leadership Avoidance clog may require both Clarify (decision rights) and Rebuild Trust (credibility restoration).
The goal is to develop a leadership rhythm that moves quickly and precisely: Identify the Clog → Select the Lever → Targeted Intervention.

parts.title: 2.3 — The 7 Strategic Unclogging Levers
guidance: ◆ Lever Selection Principle

Identifying a clog is only half the work. The real discipline is lever selection. Rarely does a clog require just one fix. If the clog is a Capability Gap, the leaders may need to Upgrade the systems while simultaneously Reinforcing the team’s skills. If the clog is Leadership Avoidance, there will likely be a need to Clarify decision rights and Rebuild Trust to move forward. Always ask: “Which lever combination addresses the root cause?”
content: Think of these seven levers as the leadership toolkit for execution architecture. They restore the conditions that allow the strategy to move through the organisation at the speed and quality intended. Each lever targets a specific dimension of the system.
Lever 01
Standardise
Ensure Consistency
Harmonises processes and service levels across teams so everyone plays by the same rules.

Variability is a silent killer of speed. By establishing a shared “way we work,” you reduce duplication and ensure every unit pulls in the same direction. Best applied to: Structural Misfit, Misaligned Metrics & Incentives, Technology / Infrastructure Lag.
Lever 02
Streamline
Increase Speed
Simplifies workflows and removes the red tape layers that add no value to execution.
Leaner processes mean faster approvals and a team that can pivot as quickly as the market demands. Best applied to: Decision Bottlenecks, Structural Misfit.
Lever 03
Clarify
Eliminate Confusion
Defines exactly who owns what, where the handoffs are, and who has the final say.

Ambiguity breeds hesitation. When people know their roles and decision rights, accountability returns and work stops getting stuck in limbo. Best applied to: Decision Bottlenecks, Structural Misfit, Leadership Avoidance.
Lever 04
Upgrade
Remove Bottlenecks
Fixes underperforming technology and infrastructure that holds execution back.

You cannot run a modern strategy on yesterday’s tools. Upgrading removes the physical and digital friction that makes scaling feel impossible. Best applied to: Technology / Infrastructure Lag, Capability Gaps.
Lever 05
Reinforce
Strengthen Behaviour
Equips the team with the skills, coaching, and confidence they need to actually deliver.
Strategy requires new behaviours. Reinforcement ensures your people are capable of making the change. Best applied to: Capability Gaps, Cultural Resistance.
Lever 06
Realign
Focus on Results
Adjusts metrics and rewards so they actually match current strategic priorities.

People do what they are measured on. When you fix the incentives, the team’s energy naturally shifts from protecting their patch to creating enterprise value. Best applied to: Misaligned Metrics & Incentives.
Lever 07
Rebuild Trust
Restore Credibility
Heals relationships and introduces the transparency needed for people to commit again.

Trust is the social grease of execution. Without it, the system seizes up. Rebuilding it restores the psychological safety required for high-stakes work. Best applied to: Cultural Resistance, Leadership Avoidance.

sections.label: Section 3 · Extrapolating — Where
sections.h2: Where Are the Highest-Flammability Clog Zones?
sections.sub: Using COMPASS as the primary diagnostic instrument to locate where execution friction is accumulating — and applying the 4-step Strategic Unclogging activation process.
slo: Evaluate where interdependent conditions are causing friction to accumulate across the enterprise.
Distinguish visible symptoms from their underlying organisational causes.

guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Extrapolating

Open with the key shift: from generic problem-solving to precise system intervention. COMPASS gives the leadership team a shared coordinate system for locating where clogs are forming, pinpointing the domain in the execution architecture where friction is accumulating.

The interpretation guidance is critical: a capability gap located in People & Capability is a skills issue; the same gap located in Systems & Execution may be an operating model issue. The combination of clog + zone provides precision that clog category alone does not. Walk through two or three examples before the 4-step activation.

For the 4-step activation: this is the procedural backbone that connects directly to the Excel Unclogging Tool participants have. Walk it as a live demonstration with one stalled KPI from the group before moving to Application.

parts.title: 3.1 — The 7 COMPASS High-Flammability Zones
content: Each clog will surface within one or more of the following COMPASS zones. By locating clogs within COMPASS, leaders move from reactive problem-solving to precise system intervention.
C
Clarity of Direction
Signals confusion, drift, or competing priorities in the strategic direction. When this zone heats up, people are unclear what the strategy actually requires of them day-to-day.
Warning signals: Strategy described differently by each leader; too many unranked priorities; teams treat strategy as an annual event not daily guidance; people wait for clarity before acting.
Most common clogs: Decision Bottlenecks, Leadership Avoidance, Cultural Resistance.
O
Organisational Alignment
Signals fragmentation across functions. When this zone heats up, different parts of the organisation are executing to different priorities or conflicting incentives.
Warning signals: KPIs conflict across functions; incentives reward wrong behaviours; silos resist shared outcomes; customer issues bounce between teams unresolved.
Most common clogs: Structural Misfit, Misaligned Metrics & Incentives, Cultural Resistance.
M
Management Discipline
Signals weak follow-through and accountability. When this zone heats up, governance is producing reports with no decisions, and performance gaps are tolerated and left uncorrected.
Warning signals: No clear review cadence; decision rights unclear; leaders tolerate repeated misses; accountability conversations avoided; teams hide problems.
Most common clogs: Decision Bottlenecks, Leadership Avoidance, Cultural Resistance.
P
People & Capability
Signals execution strain or capacity gaps. When this zone heats up, the strategy is demanding capabilities the organisation has not yet built or deployed.
Warning signals: Strategy requires skills not available; over-reliance on consultants without internal transfer; people fear speaking up; performance standards vary across teams.
Most common clogs: Capability Gaps, Leadership Avoidance, Cultural Resistance.
A
Allocation of Resources
Signals misalignment between stated priorities and actual investment decisions. When this zone heats up, money and people are flowing to the wrong places relative to the strategy.
Warning signals: Budget follows history not priorities; too many projects funded simultaneously; leaders commit to outcomes without resourcing; teams compete defensively for resources.
Most common clogs: Structural Misfit, Leadership Avoidance, Cultural Resistance.
S1
Systems & Execution
Signals operational or structural friction slowing execution throughput. When this zone heats up, the machinery of delivery is creating drag on flow.
Warning signals: Operating model doesn’t support strategic priorities; critical work delayed by approvals; tools slow delivery; leaders don’t remove blockers; firefighting feels normal.
Most common clogs: Structural Misfit, Technology / Infrastructure Lag, Leadership Avoidance.
S2
Sensing & Adaptation
Signals missed or ignored internal and external feedback. When this zone heats up, the organisation is operating on stale information and has lost its ability to adapt in real time.
Warning signals: Customer churn visible but ignored; competitor moves tracked late; leaders defend outdated forecasts; people hide bad news; teams stick to plans when reality has shifted.
Most common clogs: Capability Gaps, Leadership Avoidance, Cultural Resistance.

parts.title: 3.2 — The 4-Step Unclogging Activation
content: The Strategic Unclogging activation is triggered when a KR/KPI shows signs of execution risk. The objective is precise diagnosis of the obstruction preventing flow.
Step 1
Identify Clog Category
Step 2
Locate in COMPASS
Step 3
Trigger Lever
Step 4
Rate Severity
Select the Type of Friction
Review the 7 clog categories and select the one that best describes the execution blockage:
Structural Misfit
Capability Gaps
Decision Bottlenecks
Misaligned Metrics or Incentives
Cultural Resistance
Technology / Infrastructure Lag
Leadership Avoidance
This step establishes the type of friction affecting execution. It is the most important diagnostic step — an incorrectly classified clog will attract an incorrectly selected lever.
Pinpoint Where in the System the Clog Is Forming
Identify the relevant COMPASS zone: C · O · M · P · A · S1 · S2
The combination of clog category + COMPASS zone provides diagnostic precision:
Clog Category | COMPASS Zone | Diagnosis
Capability Gap | People & Capability | Skills or capacity issue — build or recruit
Decision Bottleneck | Management Discipline | Governance breakdown — clarify decision rights
Structural Misfit | Systems & Execution | Operating model misalignment — redesign
Cultural Resistance | Organisational Alignment | Behavioural fragmentation — reinforce + rebuild trust
Activate the Appropriate Lever
Once the clog and COMPASS zone are identified, select the intervention lever:
Standardise — establish consistent frameworks or processes
Streamline — simplify workflows or decision pathways
Clarify — define roles, ownership, and decision rights
Upgrade — modernise systems, tools, or infrastructure
Reinforce — strengthen capability through coaching or development
Realign — adjust incentives, metrics, or priorities
Rebuild Trust — restore credibility through visible leadership action
This enables rapid movement from diagnosis to intervention. The lever must be matched to the root cause.
Prioritise the Intervention
Assess the level of execution risk to determine urgency:
Low — early signal present; limited impact on momentum. Monitor and pre-empt.
Medium — clear friction affecting progress; intervention required within 5 working days.
High — significant execution risk; immediate action required; escalate to Alignment Brigade.

Severity rating allows leadership teams to prioritise interventions across the strategy portfolio. A portfolio view of all active clogs — their categories, COMPASS zones, and severity ratings — constitutes the Enterprise Unclogging Agenda.

sections.label: Section 4 · Integration — Collective
sections.sub: Building the collective discipline of normalising the unclog — where detecting and clearing execution friction becomes a shared leadership habit.
slo: Recognise why restoring execution momentum requires collective leadership stewardship.
Establish a shared leadership rhythm for surfacing and resolving friction.

guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Integration

The central shift in this zone is from my clog to our clog. Most execution blockages surface in one function but originate in another. A technology lag in IT may actually reflect a resource allocation decision in Finance. A cultural resistance in Sales may be the downstream consequence of a leadership avoidance pattern at the top. The Alignment Brigade must own the diagnostic conversation collectively.

The “see something, say something” principle is culturally important. In most organisations, surfacing a problem in someone else’s domain is politically risky. Reframe this explicitly: detecting friction early is an act of leadership stewardship.

Close this zone by having each CXO name one clog they suspect is forming outside their function — and the COMPASS zone where they believe it is accumulating. This is the seed of the Enterprise Unclogging Agenda.

parts.title: 4.1 — Normalising the Unclog: From Crisis to Habit
content: In most organisations, when execution hits a snag, the response is messy. Leaders vent in hallways, complain about “poor execution” in silos, and fixes are applied inconsistently. It is reactive, exhausting, and typically produces a cycle of constant firefighting with little genuine improvement.

The purpose of the Integration section is to standardise how the leadership team finds and fixes blockages. By using a shared unclogging process, the entire leadership team operates with a common language and a reliable toolkit. Fixing execution friction becomes a normal part of how the organisation runs.

When “unclogging” is a standard discipline, flagging a problem is no longer seen as a failure or a critique of a colleague. It is treated as valuable data. Leaders build a culture where detecting friction early is celebrated — because it is how the organisation learns to adapt.
This gives the Alignment Brigade a clear shared path:
Is there a clog?
What category does it fall into?
Which part of the system is it affecting?
Which lever do we pull to fix it?

When leaders standardise how they find and fix blockages, they develop a genuine organisational superpower: the ability to maintain the flow of strategy. They stop letting friction build up in the corners of the organisation. The result is a team that executes strategy with discipline, transparency, and a collective “we’ve got this” attitude.

parts.title: 4.2 — The “See Something, Say Something” Principle
guidance: ◆ Facilitator Exercise
Ask each CXO to complete the following statement silently, then share in the group:

“The clog I suspect is forming outside my function is [clog category] in the [COMPASS zone]. The signal I’m observing is [signal]. I’m not raising it because [barrier]. I should raise it because [consequence of not raising it].”

The barriers that emerge — political risk, uncertainty, not wanting to appear critical — are the cultural patterns that must be addressed before the unclogging discipline can become a genuine team habit.
content: Even though every KR has a specific leadership owner, blockages rarely stay in one lane. A technical delay in IT might actually be a people problem in Marketing or a process clog in Finance. Because execution is a team sport, the unclogging tool is for everyone.

If any leader sees friction forming, including outside their own area of execution, they are encouraged to surface it. This is about shared stewardship. Surfacing a blockage early is an act of leadership, ensuring that small hitches do not turn into organisation-wide delays.

parts.title: 4.3 — Enterprise Unclogging Agenda: Collective Capture
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE

Participants add their contributions to the Enterprise Unclogging Agenda in their own file. Consolidate them on a shared board by COMPASS zone and severity, and agree the top three items with named owners.
◆ Facilitator Closing Note — Integration

Close by naming the shift that has occurred. The group has moved from reacting to stalled initiatives to actively engineering the flow of execution. The Enterprise Unclogging Agenda is a leadership instrument. Each item on it represents an opportunity to restore strategic momentum before performance collapse makes the intervention far more costly.
content: The Integration section closes with each CXO contributing to a shared Enterprise Unclogging Agenda — the collective view of where clogs are forming, their severity, and the levers required. This replaces the informal “hallway complaints” with a structured, visible, collectively owned priority list.

sections.label: Section 5 · Application — In Practice
sections.sub: A structured 3-part exercise where participants practise moving from execution symptom to precise diagnosis to targeted intervention — using a real stalled KPI from their own organisation.
slo: Diagnose the root cause of a stalled priority in their current portfolio.
Determine a targeted response with a named owner, action and completion date.

guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — The Clog Clinic

This exercise is non-negotiable and must use real data. Hypothetical clogs produce hypothetical insights. The Diagnostician must bring an actual stalled KPI — one that has been visible for more than two review cycles without resolution. The discomfort of working on a real problem in front of colleagues is precisely the point.

Watch for the symptom-to-lever skip. The most common failure is jumping from observable symptom directly to lever selection without naming the clog. A lever applied to the wrong clog will not clear it — and may make the underlying problem worse. If this happens, pause and redirect: “Wait. Before we select the lever, have we correctly classified the clog? Let’s go back to Q3.”

Watch for Cultural Resistance overuse. It is the most comfortable diagnosis because it externalises the problem. Challenge it: “Is this genuinely a culture issue — or is it a Leadership Avoidance clog that has produced cultural symptoms?”

Watch for vague levers. “We’ll improve communication” is too vague to act on. A lever is a structural change — a redesigned decision right, a reset KPI, a rebuilt process, a named accountability. Push until the action is concrete enough to be owned.
Timing: 5 minutes silent prep + 30 minutes triads (10 minutes per person) + 10 minutes Alignment Brigade Challenge. Total: 45 minutes. Do not compress the triad rounds.
content: ◆ Strategic Unclogging Tool — Reference

Participants should have the S2R® Strategic Unclogging Tool (Excel) open during this exercise. The tool’s Diagnostic Form guides them through the same 4-step activation sequence used in this exercise: select COMPASS Zone → select Signal → auto-diagnose Clog → receive Lever recommendation → rate Severity. The Quick Reference tab provides the full signal library organised by zone.

parts.title: 5.1 — The Clog Clinic: Exercise Structure
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE
Give participants five minutes of silent preparation: the stalled KPI, the COMPASS zone and the observed signal. Start the triads only once every participant has prepared.
content: Part 1 · 5 min
Individual Prep
Part 2 · 30 min
Diagnostic Triads
Part 3 · 10 min
Brigade Challenge
Silent Individual Preparation
Each participant identifies one KPI or Key Result from their current portfolio that is:
Below target or stalled
Not yet resolved despite being visible for more than two review cycles
They complete three lines privately before the triad begins:
The Diagnostic Conversation — 10 Minutes Per Person
Participants work in triads: Diagnostician · Challenger · Observer. Roles rotate after each round so every participant runs the diagnostic once.
👤 Diagnostician
Presents the stalled KPI. Reasons aloud through the four questions. Must not skip Q3.
👤 Challenger
Guides through the four questions in sequence. Challenges comfortable answers. Does not give the diagnosis — draws it out.
👤 Observer
Listens and evaluates against the four criteria. Provides structured feedback after the round.
Four Questions — in sequence, without skipping:
Q1 — Where is the friction?
“Which COMPASS zone best describes where the pain is showing up — C, O, M, P, A, S1, or S2?”
Q2 — What is the signal?
“Of the signals in that zone — which one most precisely describes what you are observing?”
Q3 — What is the clog?

“Based on that signal — what type of blockage is at the root? Structure, capability, decision, metrics, culture, technology, or leadership?” The Challenger challenges: “Are you sure that’s the root — or is that the symptom of something deeper?”
Q4 — What lever would you pull?
“Given that diagnosis — what is the first action you would take? A specific action, with an owner and a date.”
The Alignment Brigade Challenge — Full Group
Each triad nominates one diagnosis to bring to the full group — ideally the one they found most difficult to crack. The nominated Diagnostician presents in 90 seconds:
“Our KR was [X]. The friction zone was [Y]. The signal was [Z]. We diagnosed [clog]. Our proposed lever is [action] — owned by [person] — by [date].”
The full group then challenges for three minutes:
Is the COMPASS zone correctly identified?
Is the clog category the root cause or just a surface symptom?
Is the lever precise enough — or is it still general pressure?
The facilitator closes each challenge with:
“What would have to be true for that lever to actually clear the clog?”

parts.title: 5.2 — Observer Evaluation Criteria
content: Criterion 01 — The Diagnostician Reasoned Through It
Did the Diagnostician go straight to the comfortable answer — or genuinely reason through the diagnostic sequence? A good diagnostic conversation shows visible thinking.
Criterion 02 — The Clog Was Distinguished from the Symptom

Was the clog correctly separated from what was initially observed? The symptom is what leadership sees first (e.g. slow delivery). The clog is the root cause (e.g. decision bottleneck). These must remain distinct.
Criterion 03 — The Challenger Used Curiosity

Did the Challenger draw out the diagnosis through questions — or push the Diagnostician toward a conclusion? A good challenger maintains diagnostic curiosity throughout and challenges without prescribing.
Criterion 04 — The Intervention Was Concrete

Did the conversation end with a specific, time-bound action that both parties understood and accepted? “We’ll improve communication” is too vague to act on. A lever is a structural change with a named owner and a date.

parts.title: Unit Summary
guidance: ◆ Facilitator Closing Note

Close by asking each leader to name one clog that has been present in their organisation for more than six months — visible, discussed, but not yet cleared. Ask them: “What has it actually cost the organisation in strategic momentum? And what is the real reason it hasn’t been cleared yet?” The answers to the second question are almost always the true clogs beneath the clogs. That conversation is the beginning of genuine execution engineering.
content: Awareness — What

A Strategic Clog is an internal blockage that prevents strategic intent from flowing into execution. The 7-clog diagnostic map — aligned to ABCV Directional Integrity — gives leaders the vocabulary to name the type of friction behind the symptom.
Intelligence — Why

Clogs are design signals. Where strategy stretches the operating system beyond its current capacity, friction will appear predictably. The three disciplines of execution engineering (identify, classify, intervene) and the 7 levers restore flow without reactive pressure.

sections.label: Section 1 · Awareness — What
sections.sub: Naming the internal blockages that prevent strategic intent from flowing into execution — and mapping the 7 clog categories to ABCV Directional Integrity.
slo: Recognise the systemic blockages that widen the gap between strategic intent and execution.

parts.title: 1.1 — What is a Strategic Clog?
content: At its simplest, a Strategic Clog is an internal blockage that prevents strategic intent from flowing into real-world execution. It is the widening gap between what we said we would do and what is actually happening.
Strategy sets the destination. Flow determines whether you have the power to arrive.

To navigate this phase of the execution climb, leadership must evolve. The role of the leadership team becomes to serve as Engineers of Execution Flow — developing the diagnostic eyes to detect clogs early, before they compound into stalled momentum or declining performance.
Every clog interferes with one or more elements of ABCV Directional Integrity:
Arena — clarity of the problem space and customer end-game
Boundaries — structural, operational, and regulatory constraints
Competition — how the organisation defines alternatives and threats
Value Proposition — how the organisation creates distinct value

When execution is clogged, strategy loses directional integrity — gradually and silently. A clog acts like a pressure distortion point: it redirects effort away from intended outcomes, weakens coherence across functions, and creates misinterpretation of strategic intent.
✎ Reflection — Strategic Clog in Your Organisation
prompts: ✎ Reflection — Strategic Clog in Your Organisation — Think of a strategy initiative that stalled in your organisation. Was the plan wrong — or was something in the system blocking its flow? What was the blockage? Could it have been named earlier?

parts.title: 1.2 — Three Observable Friction Signals
content: Three patterns signal that a clog is forming. Which do you recognise most immediately in your organisation?
Decision Paralysis
Choices that should be instinctive begin taking longer than expected, creating a bottleneck at the top.
Kinetic Misalignment
Teams move with intensity but pull in different directions, cancelling each other’s efforts.
Output–Outcome Gap
Tasks are completed and boxes checked, but the needle on actual strategic goals isn’t moving.

parts.title: 1.3 — The 7-Clog Diagnostic Map
parts.meta: ABCV-aligned · Select each clog to explore
content: Each clog category represents a distinct type of system misalignment. Select each to explore, and reflect on which clogs are currently present in your organisation.
Clog 01
Structural Misfit
Boundaries
What It Looks Like
Org design, roles, reporting lines, decision rights, or governance layers are misaligned to strategy. Structure reflects legacy priorities.
Early Warnings: Increasing coordination time; dependency on informal workarounds; escalation frequency rises; unclear ownership of outcomes.
Strategic Impact: Execution becomes disjointed; coordination costs increase; strategy cannot move coherently across the enterprise.
Reflect: Where in your structure do handoffs regularly break down? What does that tell you about the misalignment between your design and your strategy?
Clog 02
Capability Gaps
Arena
What It Looks Like
Critical capabilities required to deliver the strategy are absent, underdeveloped, or unevenly distributed across the organisation.
Early Warnings: Missed milestones; uneven performance across similar initiatives; burnout of key talent; increasing rework.
Strategic Impact: The defined arena becomes theoretical — execution lacks the capability backbone required to compete and deliver.
Reflect: Which capability does your current strategy demand that your organisation has not yet fully built? How long has that gap been visible?
Clog 03
Decision Bottlenecks
Boundaries
What It Looks Like
Decision rights are unclear, overly centralised, or embedded in outdated hierarchical processes. Authority is not aligned to execution proximity.
Early Warnings: Decision cycle times increase; growing backlog of unresolved issues; teams hesitate to act without approval.
Strategic Impact: Decision flow is constrained, weakening execution rhythm. The organisation loses responsiveness.
Reflect: Where in your organisation are decisions taking longer than the pace of strategy demands? What is the cost of that delay?
Clog 04
Misaligned Metrics & Incentives
Value Proposition
What It Looks Like
KPIs, scorecards, and reward systems reinforce behaviours that conflict with strategic intent. Legacy metrics remain active post-strategy shift.
Early Warnings: High KPI achievement with weak strategic progress; conflicting performance narratives; misalignment between reported success and actual outcomes.
Strategic Impact: Effort redirected toward what is measured, whether or not it creates value. The organisation produces activity without differentiated strategic outcomes.
Reflect: Which metrics in your current scorecard are rewarding behaviours that actually conflict with your strategic priorities?
Clog 05
Cultural Resistance
Value Proposition
What It Looks Like
Deeply embedded beliefs, norms, and habits contradict the behavioural shifts required by the strategy. Informal culture overrides formal direction.
Early Warnings: Low engagement in strategic initiatives; limited experimentation; silence in critical conversations; informal narratives contradicting strategy.
Strategic Impact: The organisation cannot consistently deliver intended value because behaviour does not align with strategic intent.
Reflect: Is what you are observing genuinely a culture issue — or is it a Leadership Avoidance issue that has produced cultural symptoms?
Clog 06
Technology / Infrastructure Lag
Competition
What It Looks Like
Legacy systems, fragmented platforms, and poorly integrated infrastructure cannot support execution demands. Data architecture is incomplete or delayed.
Early Warnings: Data inconsistencies; long reporting cycles; operational errors increase at scale; inability to track real-time performance.
Strategic Impact: The organisation loses execution speed and intelligence; cannot respond, scale, or compete against more technologically enabled alternatives.
Reflect: Which technology or infrastructure constraint is most directly limiting your ability to execute the strategy at the speed it demands?
Clog 07
Leadership Avoidance
Arena + Boundaries
What It Looks Like
Leaders avoid confronting trade-offs, underperformance, structural misalignment, or difficult decisions required for strategy execution.
Early Warnings: Recurring strategic issues across multiple cycles; low trust in leadership decisions; ambiguity in direction; declining ownership across teams.
Strategic Impact: Strategic clarity erodes as unresolved tensions accumulate. The organisation drifts between priorities, weakening both focus and execution discipline.
Reflect: What difficult decision has your leadership team been circling for more than two cycles without closure? What is the real cost of continued avoidance?

sections.label: Section 2 · Intelligence — Why
sections.h2: Why Clogs Are Predictable Features of Execution
sections.sub: Understanding why execution friction is the inevitable consequence of system misalignment — and the 7 levers that restore execution flow.
slo: Explain why execution friction is a predictable consequence of strategy stretching the operating system.
Recognise the leadership disciplines that detect and resolve friction early.

parts.title: 2.1 — Clogs Are Design Signals
content: Execution breakdowns usually occur because the organisation’s structure, capabilities, behaviours, or systems have not yet adapted to the strategy. The clog is the signal that the system requires adjustment.

Clogs emerge precisely where strategy stretches the existing operating system beyond its current design capacity. They are predictable. This transforms the role of the executive team: defining direction and ensuring the operating system can carry that direction without excessive friction.
The mindset shift: move from asking “Why is the strategy failing?” to asking “Where is the system not yet designed to carry the strategy?”
✎ Reflection — Where Is Your System Not Yet Ready?
prompts: ✎ Reflection — Where Is Your System Not Yet Ready? — Given your current strategic direction — which element of your operating system is most likely to create friction? (Structure / Decision rights / Culture / Metrics / Capability / Technology) Why is this predictable given your strategy?

parts.title: 2.2 — Three Disciplines of Execution Engineering
content: Discipline 1
Early Identification
Discipline 2
Accurate Classification
Discipline 3
Targeted Intervention
Detect Signals Before They Compound

Leaders must detect the signals that indicate friction is forming. Bottlenecks, repeated coordination failures, declining execution speed, or growing ambiguity in decision rights are all early indicators that a clog is emerging.

The strategic value of early identification is significant. A clog detected when it is a friction signal requires a targeted structural adjustment. The same clog discovered six months later, after it has compounded into a systemic execution failure, requires a crisis response. The cost — in time, capital, and leadership credibility — is vastly different.
This discipline requires leaders to build signal literacy: the ability to read organisational patterns as early indicators of structural misalignment.
Name the Clog Precisely Before Intervening

Each clog belongs to a specific category of organisational friction. Structural misfit, capability gaps, decision bottlenecks, misaligned incentives, cultural resistance, technological constraints, or leadership avoidance each require fundamentally different forms of intervention.

The most common diagnostic failure is applying the wrong lever to a correctly identified symptom. A leader who observes “slow execution” and responds by adding resources is applying a capability lever to what may be a decision bottleneck. The additional resources do not accelerate execution because the constraint is approval latency.
Accurate classification requires resisting the impulse to solve before diagnosing. The first question is “What type of friction is this, and what does it tell us about the system?”
Pull the Right Lever with Precision

Once the clog is identified and classified, it must be addressed through the appropriate strategic lever. Clogs rarely clear themselves through trying harder or working more hours. They require a deliberate adjustment to the organisation’s structural, behavioural, and operational settings.

Targeted intervention means matching the lever to the root cause. It also means accepting that rarely does a single clog require just one fix. A Capability Gap may require both Upgrade (systems) and Reinforce (skills). A Leadership Avoidance clog may require both Clarify (decision rights) and Rebuild Trust (credibility restoration).
The goal is to develop a leadership rhythm that moves quickly and precisely: Identify the Clog → Select the Lever → Targeted Intervention.

parts.title: 2.3 — The 7 Strategic Unclogging Levers
content: These seven levers are the leadership toolkit for execution architecture. They restore the conditions that allow the strategy to move through the organisation at the speed and quality intended.
Lever 01
Standardise
Ensure Consistency
Harmonises processes and service levels across teams so everyone plays by the same rules. Reduces duplication and ensures every unit pulls in the same direction.
Apply when: Variability across teams is creating drag. Best for: Structural Misfit, Misaligned Metrics, Tech Lag.
Lever 02
Streamline
Increase Speed
Simplifies workflows and removes bureaucratic layers that add no value. Leaner processes mean faster approvals and greater strategic agility.
Apply when: Approval processes are creating latency. Best for: Decision Bottlenecks, Structural Misfit.
Lever 03
Clarify
Eliminate Confusion
Defines who owns what, where the handoffs are, and who has the final say. When people know their roles and decision rights, accountability returns.
Apply when: Ownership ambiguity is causing hesitation. Best for: Decision Bottlenecks, Structural Misfit, Leadership Avoidance.
Lever 04
Upgrade
Remove Bottlenecks
Fixes underperforming technology and infrastructure that holds execution back. You cannot run a modern strategy on yesterday’s tools.
Apply when: Systems are creating friction that blocks flow. Best for: Technology / Infrastructure Lag, Capability Gaps.
Lever 05
Reinforce
Strengthen Behaviour
Equips the team with the skills, coaching, and confidence needed to deliver. Strategy requires new behaviours — reinforcement ensures people are capable as well as willing.
Apply when: Skills or confidence are the limiting factor. Best for: Capability Gaps, Cultural Resistance.
Lever 06
Realign
Focus on Results
Adjusts metrics and rewards so they match current strategic priorities. People do what they are measured on — fix the incentives and the energy shifts.
Apply when: Effort is flowing only to what is measured. Best for: Misaligned Metrics & Incentives.
Lever 07
Rebuild Trust
Restore Credibility
Heals relationships and introduces the transparency needed for people to commit again. Trust is the social grease of execution — without it, the system seizes up.
Apply when: Psychological safety or leadership credibility is the constraint. Best for: Cultural Resistance, Leadership Avoidance.
✎ Reflection — Your Lever
prompts: ✎ Reflection — Your Lever — For the clog you identified in Awareness: Which primary lever would you pull? Which secondary lever would you combine it with? Why this combination?

sections.label: Section 3 · Extrapolating — Where
sections.h2: Where Are the Highest-Flammability Clog Zones?
sections.sub: Using COMPASS as the primary diagnostic instrument to locate where execution friction is accumulating — and applying the 4-step activation process.
slo: Evaluate where interdependent conditions are causing friction to accumulate across the enterprise.

parts.title: 3.1 — The 7 COMPASS High-Flammability Zones
content: By locating clogs within COMPASS, you move from reactive problem-solving to precise system intervention. Select each zone to explore where friction typically accumulates.
C
Clarity of Direction
Signals confusion, drift, or competing priorities. When this zone heats up, people are unclear what strategy requires of them day-to-day.
Warning signals: Strategy described differently by each leader; too many unranked priorities; teams treat strategy as annual event; people wait for clarity before acting.
O
Organisational Alignment
Signals fragmentation across functions. Different parts of the organisation execute to different priorities or conflicting incentives.
Warning signals: KPIs conflict across functions; incentives reward wrong behaviours; silos resist shared outcomes; customer issues bounce between teams.
M
Management Discipline
Signals weak follow-through and accountability. Governance produces reports with no decisions, and performance gaps are tolerated and left uncorrected.
Warning signals: No clear review cadence; decision rights unclear; leaders tolerate repeated misses; accountability conversations avoided.
P
People & Capability
Signals execution strain or capacity gaps. Strategy is demanding capabilities the organisation has not yet built or deployed.
Warning signals: Strategy requires skills not available; over-reliance on consultants without transfer; people fear speaking up; performance standards vary.
A
Allocation of Resources
Signals misalignment between stated priorities and actual investment decisions. Money and people are flowing to the wrong places relative to strategy.
Warning signals: Budget follows history not priorities; too many projects funded simultaneously; leaders commit to outcomes without resourcing.
S1
Systems & Execution
Signals operational or structural friction slowing execution throughput. The machinery of delivery is creating drag on flow.
Warning signals: Operating model doesn’t support strategic priorities; critical work delayed by approvals; tools slow delivery; firefighting feels normal.
S2
Sensing & Adaptation
Signals missed or ignored feedback. The organisation is operating on stale information and has lost its ability to adapt in real time.
Warning signals: Customer churn visible but ignored; competitor moves tracked late; leaders defend outdated forecasts; people hide bad news; teams stick to plans when reality has shifted.

parts.title: 3.2 — The 4-Step Unclogging Activation
content: When a KR/KPI shows signs of execution risk, activate this 4-step diagnostic sequence. The objective is precise diagnosis of the obstruction preventing flow.
Step 1
Identify Clog
Step 2
Locate in COMPASS
Step 3
Trigger Lever
Step 4
Rate Severity
Select the Type of Friction

Review the 7 clog categories and select the one that best describes the execution blockage. This is the most important step — an incorrectly classified clog will attract an incorrectly selected lever.
Ask: “Is this a structure problem, a capability problem, a decision problem, a metrics problem, a culture problem, a technology problem, or a leadership problem?”
Pinpoint Where in the System
Identify the COMPASS zone where the clog is forming. The combination of clog + zone provides diagnostic precision:
Clog Category | COMPASS Zone | Diagnosis
Capability Gap | People & Capability | Skills or capacity issue
Decision Bottleneck | Management Discipline | Governance breakdown
Structural Misfit | Systems & Execution | Operating model misalignment
Cultural Resistance | Organisational Alignment | Behavioural fragmentation
Select and Apply the Lever
Match the lever to the root cause. The lever must address what is actually blocking flow.
Standardise — establish consistent frameworks
Streamline — simplify workflows
Clarify — define roles and decision rights
Upgrade — modernise systems or infrastructure
Reinforce — build capability through coaching
Realign — adjust incentives and metrics
Rebuild Trust — restore credibility through visible action
Prioritise the Intervention
Low — early signal; monitor and pre-empt
Medium — clear friction; act within 5 working days
High — significant risk; escalate to Alignment Brigade immediately
Severity rating allows the team to prioritise across the full strategy portfolio and build the Enterprise Unclogging Agenda.

parts.title: 4.1 — Normalising the Unclog: From Crisis to Habit
content: The purpose of the Integration section is to standardise how the leadership team finds and fixes blockages. By using a shared unclogging process, the entire Alignment Brigade operates with a common language and a reliable toolkit. Fixing execution friction becomes a normal part of how the organisation runs.

When “unclogging” is a standard discipline, flagging a problem is no longer seen as a failure or a critique of a colleague. It is treated as valuable data. Detecting friction early is an act of leadership stewardship.
The shared diagnostic path: Is there a clog? → What category? → Which COMPASS zone? → Which lever?

parts.title: 4.2 — The “See Something, Say Something” Principle
content: Even though every KR has a specific leadership owner, blockages rarely stay in one lane. A technical delay in IT might actually be a people problem in Marketing or a process clog in Finance. Because execution is a team sport, the unclogging tool is for everyone.

If any leader sees friction forming, including outside their own area of execution, they are encouraged to surface it. This is about shared stewardship. Surfacing a blockage early is an act of leadership, ensuring that small hitches do not turn into organisation-wide delays.
